header_copy.Pstw01: welcome to the world, little one.
header_copy.Pstw02: two weeks of getting to know each other.
header_copy.Pstm23: is it time for a big bed?
header_copy.Pstm60: five years. Look how far you've come.

body_copy.Pstw01: Your baby can see most clearly at about 20 to 30cm, which is roughly the distance to your face when you hold them to feed. That's why they'll study you so closely.
body_copy.Pstw02: Most babies lose a little weight in the first few days, then get back to their birth weight by around two weeks. Your midwife or health visitor will keep an eye on this for you.
body_copy.Pstw03: Babies often have a growth spurt at around three weeks. You might notice your baby feeding more often and being a bit more unsettled for a few days. It's normal and it passes.
body_copy.Pstw04: Short spells on their tummy while awake help your baby build the neck and shoulder muscles they'll need for rolling and sitting. A few minutes a few times a day is plenty to start.
body_copy.Pstw05: Your baby is spending more time awake and alert. They may turn towards your voice and follow a face or a bright object with their eyes for a short moment.
body_copy.Pstw06: Many babies give their first social smile around six weeks. It's different from the windy grins of the early days, as it's a response to you.
body_copy.Pstw07: Your baby can now recognise familiar faces and voices, and may calm down more quickly when you pick them up. They're learning who their people are.
body_copy.Pstw08: Your baby got some protection from you before birth, but it fades over the first few months. Their first vaccinations help their immune system learn to protect them.
body_copy.Pstw09: Around now, many babies discover their own hands and can spend ages staring at them. It's a big step as they work out that those fingers belong to them.
body_copy.Pstw10: Those little coos and gurgles are your baby's first attempts at chatting. When you answer back and pause, you're teaching them how conversation works.
body_copy.Pstw11: During tummy time your baby may now lift their head and chest up on their forearms. Their neck is getting much stronger, so they need less support when held.
body_copy.Pstw12: By around 12 weeks, many babies have more settled patterns of sleeping and feeding. Every baby is different, so don't worry if yours isn't there yet.
body_copy.Pstw13: Around three months, many babies start to laugh out loud. Silly noises, gentle tickles and peekaboo are usually a hit.
body_copy.Pstw14: Your baby's brain is making new connections faster than at any other time in life. Everyday moments like talking, singing and cuddling help build them.
body_copy.Pstw15: Many babies have a growth spurt between three and four months. They may want to feed more often for a few days and could be more unsettled.
body_copy.Pstw16: Your baby is now likely to put everything in their mouth. It's how they explore texture and shape, so keep small objects well out of reach.
body_copy.Pstw17: Babies usually start rolling between four and six months, often from tummy to back first. Lots of tummy time helps them build the strength they need.
body_copy.Pstw18: Most babies are ready to start solid food at around six months. Until then, breast milk or formula gives them everything they need.
body_copy.Pstw19: For babies, play is serious work. Every time they reach, grab, shake or chew a toy, they're learning about cause and effect.
body_copy.Pstw20: Around five months, some babies begin to respond to their name by turning their head or looking at you. Keep using it often.
body_copy.Pstw21: Milestones are a guide, not a deadline. Some babies sit early and crawl late, others do the opposite. What matters is steady progress over time.
body_copy.Pstw22: Your baby is learning to grab objects with their whole hand and pass them from one hand to the other. These skills will lead to finger feeding later on.
body_copy.Pstw23: Your baby may be rolling, wriggling and pivoting already. Crawling usually starts between six and ten months, but some babies skip it altogether.
body_copy.Pstw24: Your baby has roughly doubled their birth weight by now. They may be sitting with a little support and showing real interest in what you're eating.
body_copy.Pstw25: Some babies are busy on the physical side while others focus on sounds or social skills. Development rarely happens evenly across everything at once.
body_copy.Pstw26: Your baby has thousands of taste buds and is ready to learn about new flavours. Offering a wide variety early can help them accept different foods.
body_copy.Pstw27: When your baby laughs at peekaboo, they're starting to understand that things still exist when they can't see them. It's an important early thinking skill.
body_copy.Pstw28: Even without many teeth, your baby can mash soft lumps with their gums. Moving on to textured food helps develop the muscles they'll use for speech.
body_copy.Pstw29: Babies find comfort in predictable patterns. A similar order to your day, like milk, play, nap, can help your baby know what's coming.
body_copy.Pstw30: Your baby is learning by watching and copying you. Waving bye-bye and clapping hands may come a little later, but you can start showing them now.
body_copy.Pstw31: Your baby is learning all the time, from the sounds in the supermarket to the feel of grass. Real life is the best classroom at this age.
body_copy.Pstw32: Around eight months, babies are learning to crawl, pull up and understand more. All that brain activity can disrupt sleep for a while.
body_copy.Pstw33: Getting upset when you leave the room shows your baby has formed a strong bond with you. They don't yet understand that you'll always come back.
body_copy.Pstw34: Your baby is starting to explore further from you, but will often look back to check you're there. You're their safe base.
body_copy.Pstw35: Smiling, babbling, reaching for you and settling in your arms are all signs of a contented baby. Every baby has grumpy days too.
body_copy.Pstw36: Babies move between light and deep sleep throughout the night. Learning to settle themselves between cycles is a skill that takes time.
body_copy.Pstw37: Time on their tummy helps your baby build the strength for crawling, pulling up and eventually walking. It still counts, even at nine months.
body_copy.Pstw38: Once babies can pull themselves up, many start cruising, which means stepping sideways while holding on to furniture. It's an important step towards walking.
body_copy.Pstw39: Your baby understands far more than they can say. They may respond to simple words like 'no' or 'bye-bye' and look at familiar objects when you name them.
body_copy.Pstw40: Your baby is learning cause and effect, which is why they might drop food from the highchair again and again to see what happens.
body_copy.Pstw41: Many babies are now using their thumb and finger to pick up small things, known as the pincer grip. Perfect for peas, and unfortunately for crumbs on the floor.
body_copy.Pstw42: Your baby now knows the difference between familiar people and strangers. Being shy or upset around new faces is a normal stage of development.
body_copy.Pstw43: Your baby is starting to solve simple problems, like pulling a blanket to reach a toy or finding something you've hidden under a cup.
body_copy.Pstw44: Your baby is getting ready for big changes in the next few months, including first steps and first words. Their personality is really shining through.
body_copy.Pstw45: Most babies take their first steps between 9 and 18 months, so there's a wide range of normal. Many walk around their first birthday.
body_copy.Pstw46: Some babies say words early, others walk early. Development is uneven, and many babies catch up quickly once they're ready.
body_copy.Pstw47: Your baby enjoys watching other children and may babble or wave at them. True playing together comes later, but these early moments matter.
body_copy.Pstw48: Most babies have roughly tripled their birth weight by their first birthday. In just a year, your baby has learned to smile, laugh, sit, eat and move.
body_copy.Pstw49: Many babies say their first word around their first birthday. Sounds like 'ba' for ball or 'da' for dog count as words if they use them consistently.
body_copy.Pstw50: Most one-year-olds still need two naps a day. Many move to one nap somewhere between 12 and 18 months.
body_copy.Pstw51: Lots of babies start nursery or a childminder around their first birthday. It can take a few weeks for them to settle, and that's normal.
body_copy.Pstw52: From one year, whole cow's milk can be your baby's main drink. It's a good time to move from bottles to an open or free-flow cup too.
body_copy.Pstw53: Your baby is officially a toddler. Over the next few months they'll likely start walking, say a few more words and show more independence.
body_copy.Pstw54: Your toddler wants to explore everything. Expect them to empty cupboards, climb on things and test what objects can do.
body_copy.Pstw55: Through play, toddlers learn about size, shape, colour and how things work. They love repetition, so the same game ten times is good for them.
body_copy.Pstw56: Your toddler can move fast and reach more than ever. They don't understand danger yet, so keeping them safe is all about the environment around them.
body_copy.Pstw57: Toddlers often prefer the box to the toy. Everyday objects can provide hours of fun and learning.
body_copy.Pstw58: At this age, toddlers usually play side by side rather than together. This is called parallel play and it's an important step.
body_copy.Pstw59: New skills like walking and talking can disrupt sleep. Teething, illness and changes in routine can all cause temporary wobbles too.
body_copy.Pstw60: Toddlers don't yet understand that other people have feelings and wants. Sharing will come with time and lots of practice.
body_copy.Pstw61: Your toddler studies everything you do, from how you talk to how you handle frustration. They're learning how the world works from you.
body_copy.Pstw62: Most children move from a cot to a bed somewhere between 18 months and 3 years. There's no rush if your toddler is happy and safe in their cot.
body_copy.Pstw63: Tantrums happen because toddlers have big emotions but not the words to express them. Their brains are still learning to manage frustration.
body_copy.Pstw64: Night terrors happen in deep sleep, often early in the night. Your toddler may scream or thrash but won't remember it in the morning.
body_copy.Pstw65: Toddlers need around 11 to 14 hours of sleep in 24 hours, including naps. Busy days with lots of stimulation can make them overtired.
body_copy.Pstw66: Your toddler is unique. What works for one family doesn't always work for another, and that's completely fine.
body_copy.Pstw67: Your toddler is becoming more independent every day. They can likely walk, feed themselves and let you know what they want.
body_copy.Pstw68: Toddlers need small, frequent meals and snacks. Their tummies are small, so every bite counts.
body_copy.Pstw69: Your toddler is more confident with new people and places than a few months ago. Time at nursery or with a childminder can help them grow socially.
body_copy.Pstw70: Many toddlers have a vocabulary of up to 20 words by 18 months and understand far more. Some say fewer, and that can still be normal.
body_copy.Pstw71: Your toddler can play on their own for short periods. Building this skill helps them develop focus and creativity.
body_copy.Pstw72: Toddlers learn a lot from watching other children. Time with friends helps them develop social and language skills.
body_copy.Pstw73: Your toddler has their own personality, preferences and pace. Following their lead often works better than any rulebook.
body_copy.Pstw74: Toddlers love to help, even if it takes longer. Giving them small jobs builds confidence and independence.
body_copy.Pstw75: Your toddler is fascinated by the world and is starting to point and ask in their own way. Answering them builds language and curiosity.
body_copy.Pstw76: Toddlers thrive on routine and predictability. A familiar pattern on working days helps them feel safe.
body_copy.Pstw77: Toddlers still wake at night sometimes. It can be due to teething, illness, dreams or just wanting you.
body_copy.Pstw78: Most children are ready for potty training between 2 and 3 years old. Some show signs earlier, others later.
body_copy.Pstm19: It's very common for toddlers to become fussy around now. It's a normal stage as they learn to be more independent.
body_copy.Pstm20: Toddlers often push back at bedtime as they test their independence. A calm, predictable routine helps them feel secure.
body_copy.Pstm21: Your toddler is becoming more aware of their body. They may tell you when their nappy is wet or hide when they're doing a poo.
body_copy.Pstm22: Sharing is hard for toddlers because they don't yet fully understand other people's feelings. It gets easier with practice.
body_copy.Pstm23: Some toddlers are excited about a big bed, others are nervous. Involving them in the move can help.
body_copy.Pstm24: Many two-year-olds can put two words together, like 'more milk' or 'daddy gone'. Their understanding is growing every day.
body_copy.Pstm25: Toddlers are more likely to try food they've helped prepare. Simple jobs like washing veg or stirring can make a big difference.
body_copy.Pstm26: Tantrums often peak around two. Your toddler wants independence but doesn't have the skills or words yet.
body_copy.Pstm27: Toddlers feel safer with clear, consistent boundaries. They'll still test them, which is part of learning.
body_copy.Pstm28: Reading together builds vocabulary, listening skills and imagination. It's also a lovely way to connect.
body_copy.Pstm29: Outdoor play helps toddlers develop balance, coordination and confidence. Fresh air can help with sleep too.
body_copy.Pstm30: Your toddler's personality is really shining through now. They have clear likes, dislikes and opinions.
body_copy.Pstm31: Your toddler is becoming more independent and can do more for themselves, like putting on shoes or washing their hands.
body_copy.Pstm32: Booster vaccines help top up your child's protection as they get ready for nursery and school.
body_copy.Pstm33: A consistent bedtime routine helps your toddler feel safe and ready for sleep.
body_copy.Pstm34: Toddlers can enjoy holidays, especially when routines are kept as familiar as possible.
body_copy.Pstm35: Your toddler is starting to understand simple reasons, like 'we hold hands because the road is busy'.
body_copy.Pstm36: Many three-year-olds can speak in short sentences and ask lots of questions. 'Why?' might become a favourite word.
body_copy.Pstm37: As imagination develops, fears like the dark or monsters can appear. This is a normal part of development.
body_copy.Pstm38: Three-year-olds love to help and feel important. Small jobs build confidence and independence.
body_copy.Pstm39: Fussy eating is common in preschoolers. Most children grow out of it with time and patience.
body_copy.Pstm40: Children develop at their own pace, whatever their sex. Interests and skills vary from child to child.
body_copy.Pstm41: School readiness isn't about reading or writing. It's about independence, listening and getting along with others.
body_copy.Pstm42: Accidents and setbacks are common, especially during times of change like starting nursery or a new sibling arriving.
body_copy.Pstm43: Preschoolers are getting better at sharing and taking turns, but it still takes practice.
body_copy.Pstm44: Preschoolers can be very persuasive. Asking again and again is their way of testing limits.
body_copy.Pstm45: Your preschooler is learning all the time, from nursery to the supermarket. Everyday moments are full of learning.
body_copy.Pstm46: Preschoolers thrive on routine. Knowing what's happening each day helps them feel secure.
body_copy.Pstm47: Siblings will argue, it's a normal part of growing up. It's how they learn to share, negotiate and solve problems.
body_copy.Pstm48: Four-year-olds are curious, creative and full of questions. They're getting ready for big changes like starting school.
body_copy.Pstm49: Creativity helps children express themselves and develop problem-solving skills. Mess is part of the fun.
body_copy.Pstm50: Children don't need expensive toys to have fun. Their imagination can turn anything into a game.
body_copy.Pstm51: Play helps children develop language, social skills, creativity and problem-solving. It's how they make sense of the world.
body_copy.Pstm52: Children feel more secure when the adults caring for them are consistent and respectful towards each other.
body_copy.Pstm53: Cooking together teaches children about measuring, counting and following instructions, plus it's fun.
body_copy.Pstm54: When children feel listened to, it builds their confidence and helps them share their feelings.
body_copy.Pstm55: Children can start learning about money through play, like playing shops or saving coins in a jar.
body_copy.Pstm56: Preschoolers are learning how to be a good friend. Sometimes they'll be unkind or experience unkindness from others.
body_copy.Pstm57: Children love new experiences. Holidays can help build confidence and create lasting memories.
body_copy.Pstm58: Outdoor play helps children develop confidence, coordination and a love of nature.
body_copy.Pstm59: Spending time together as a family helps children feel secure and loved.
body_copy.Pstm60: Your child has grown from a tiny baby into a curious, confident little person. Five years of growing, learning and exploring.

title.Pstw01: Getting feeding off to a good start
title.Pstw50: Signs they're ready for one nap
title.Pstw62: When to move to a bed
title.Pstw64: What to do during a night terror

body_copy.Pstw01: Newborns feed little and often, usually 8 to 12 times in 24 hours. Whether you're breastfeeding, formula feeding or doing both, your midwife can help with positioning and latch. Wet and dirty nappies are a good sign your baby is getting enough.
body_copy.Pstw02: Your health visitor usually visits between 10 and 14 days after birth. They'll weigh your baby, talk about feeding and sleep and check how you're doing. It's a good time to ask anything at all, nothing is too small.
body_copy.Pstw03: Some evenings your baby may want to feed almost constantly. This is called cluster feeding and it's especially common during growth spurts. It doesn't mean you don't have enough milk, it's how babies build up your supply.
body_copy.Pstw04: Lay your baby on their tummy on your chest or a play mat when they're awake and you're watching. Start with a minute or two and build up. Always put them on their back to sleep.
body_copy.Pstw05: Your baby loves the sound of your voice. Chatting, singing and describing what you're doing all help their brain develop, even though they can't reply yet. It doesn't matter what you say.
body_copy.Pstw06: Your baby will have a physical check, usually with your GP, looking at their eyes, heart, hips and more. You should also be offered your own postnatal check around now to see how you're recovering.
body_copy.Pstw07: Babies tell you what they need through their body language. Turning away or arching their back can mean they need a break. Rooting, hand-to-mouth and lip smacking are early hunger signs.
body_copy.Pstw08: Your baby will be offered their first vaccinations at 8 weeks, including the 6-in-1, MenB and rotavirus. Feeding or cuddling straight after can help settle them. A mild temperature afterwards is common.
body_copy.Pstw09: Simple play is perfect. High-contrast pictures, your face, a rattle or a gentle song all help your baby's senses develop. Short bursts are best, so stop when they look away.
body_copy.Pstw10: Copy your baby's sounds, then wait to see if they reply. Face-to-face time, nursery rhymes and talking through your day all build early language skills, long before first words.
body_copy.Pstw11: Your baby is starting to swipe at objects and may hold a toy if you put it in their hand. Dangling toys over a play mat gives them something to aim for.
body_copy.Pstw12: At 12 weeks your baby will be offered their second 6-in-1, MenB and rotavirus vaccines. Have a cuddle and a feed ready afterwards, and keep an eye on any temperature.
body_copy.Pstw13: Your baby is more awake and interested in what's around them. Lie them on their back or tummy with toys nearby, and let them watch you as you move around the room.
body_copy.Pstw14: You don't need fancy toys. Reading board books, describing what you see on a walk and responding to their sounds all help your baby learn. Repetition is good for them.
body_copy.Pstw15: Around four months, some babies start waking more at night as their sleep patterns mature. It can feel like a step backwards, but it's a normal stage of development.
body_copy.Pstw16: At 16 weeks your baby will be offered their third 6-in-1 vaccine and the pneumococcal vaccine. A little fussiness afterwards is normal. Plenty of cuddles and feeds will help.
body_copy.Pstw17: Once your baby can roll, never leave them alone on a raised surface like a bed or changing table. Change nappies on the floor if you can, and keep a hand on them at all times.
body_copy.Pstw18: Look for three signs together: your baby can stay in a sitting position and hold their head steady, can pick up food and put it in their mouth, and can swallow food rather than push it back out.
body_copy.Pstw19: Fill a bottle with rice and seal it tightly for a shaker, show them their reflection, or let them feel different textures like a soft scarf or a crinkly bag.
body_copy.Pstw20: Over the next few weeks your baby may sit with less support, start babbling sounds like 'ba' and 'da' and get ready for their first tastes of food.
body_copy.Pstw21: Health visitors look at broad ranges rather than exact ages. If you have a worry about your baby's development, it's always fine to ask, and the earlier the better.
body_copy.Pstw22: Offer toys of different shapes and sizes, like soft blocks, rings and crinkly books. Let your baby explore safely and resist the urge to help too quickly.
body_copy.Pstw23: Get down to your baby's level to spot hazards. Secure heavy furniture to the wall, cover sockets, tie up blind cords and move cleaning products out of reach.
body_copy.Pstw24: Around six months is the recommended time to introduce food alongside breast milk or formula. Start with single vegetables, soft fruit and finger foods. Mess is all part of it.
body_copy.Pstw25: If your baby isn't reaching for toys, doesn't respond to sounds or seems stiff or floppy, mention it to your health visitor. Most of the time it's reassurance you'll get, but it's always worth asking.
body_copy.Pstw26: Try soft cooked vegetables like broccoli, carrot and sweet potato, then fruit. Avoid salt, sugar, honey and whole nuts. Always stay with your baby when they're eating.
body_copy.Pstw27: Babies love the unexpected. Peekaboo, gentle tickles, funny noises and exaggerated faces are classics for a reason. Repeat what works, they'll love it every time.
body_copy.Pstw28: Try mashing rather than blending, and offer soft finger foods they can hold. Gagging is normal as they learn and is different from choking. Learning basic first aid can give you confidence.
body_copy.Pstw29: Prep bottles or snacks the night before, keep a nappy kit in every room you use, and batch cook when you can. Lower your standards for the rest, it's survival mode.
body_copy.Pstw30: Show your baby simple actions like waving, clapping and blowing kisses, and say the words as you do them. Action songs are perfect for this.
body_copy.Pstw31: Talk about what you see, point and name things, and give your baby time outdoors. Books, songs and lots of chatter matter more than any app or gadget.
body_copy.Pstw32: Stick to a calm, consistent bedtime routine and keep night wakings quiet and dull. Practising new skills in the day can help them settle at night. It usually passes in a few weeks.
body_copy.Pstw33: Practise short separations, always say goodbye rather than sneaking off, and keep handovers calm and quick. Games like peekaboo help them learn that you come back.
body_copy.Pstw34: Give your baby space to try new things, praise their efforts and stay close by. Letting them have a go, even if they wobble, helps them learn what they can do.
body_copy.Pstw35: A happy baby is curious, responds to you and enjoys interacting. Crying is how they communicate, so it doesn't mean they're unhappy. If your baby seems unwell or not themselves, trust your instincts and get advice.
body_copy.Pstw36: A predictable routine, a dark room and putting your baby down drowsy but awake can all help. If you want to try a sleep training method, choose one that feels right for your family.
body_copy.Pstw37: Give your baby plenty of time on the floor rather than in seats or carriers. Tunnels, cushions to climb over and toys just out of reach all encourage movement.
body_copy.Pstw38: Check that furniture is stable and anchored, move sharp-cornered items and keep hot drinks out of reach. Bare feet are best for learning balance indoors.
body_copy.Pstw39: Your health visitor will offer a development review around now. They'll look at how your baby moves, plays and communicates, and you can ask about anything.
body_copy.Pstw40: Keep it simple: remove the temptation, redirect to something else and say 'no' calmly for anything dangerous. Babies this age don't understand rules yet, so consistency is key.
body_copy.Pstw41: Your baby may be crawling, pulling up, babbling 'mama' or 'dada' and pointing at things. Every baby is different, so look for progress rather than ticking boxes.
body_copy.Pstw42: Let your baby warm up in your arms, and ask visitors to give them time before picking them up. Don't force cuddles, they'll come round in their own time.
body_copy.Pstw43: Hide a toy under a cup, let them post objects into a box or play with stacking cups. Simple puzzles and naming things as you go both help their brain grow.
body_copy.Pstw44: Speak to your health visitor if your baby isn't babbling, doesn't respond to their name, isn't bearing weight on their legs or has lost skills they had before.
body_copy.Pstw45: Hold their hands to help them practise, offer a sturdy push-along toy and let them go barefoot indoors. Shoes are only needed once they're walking outside.
body_copy.Pstw46: If you're worried, talk to your health visitor or GP. They can check your baby and, if needed, refer you for extra support. Early help can make a big difference.
body_copy.Pstw47: Baby groups, play dates and time with family give your baby chances to watch and learn from others. Name feelings as they happen to help them understand emotions.
body_copy.Pstw48: Around their first birthday, your baby will be offered vaccines including MMRV, MenB and pneumococcal boosters. Book the appointment soon after they turn one.
body_copy.Pstw49: Talk to your baby throughout the day, name things they look at and repeat back what they say with the right word. Reading and singing together help too.
body_copy.Pstw50: If your baby takes ages to settle for one nap, or a second nap is pushing bedtime late, they may be ready. Try moving to one longer nap around lunchtime.
body_copy.Pstw51: Settling-in sessions, a comforter from home and a quick, calm goodbye all help. Ask your setting for a photo or update in the first few days if it helps you feel reassured.
body_copy.Pstw52: Using a cup is better for your toddler's teeth. Start by offering their milk in a free-flow cup at one meal, then gradually swap the rest.
body_copy.Pstw53: At this age many toddlers are pulling to stand, cruising or taking first steps, saying one or two words and pointing to show you things. It's a guide, not a test.
body_copy.Pstw54: In the coming months your toddler may walk confidently, start stacking blocks, scribble with crayons and learn new words every week.
body_copy.Pstw55: Try posting toys through a cardboard box, filling and emptying containers, splashing in the bath or making music with pots and wooden spoons.
body_copy.Pstw56: Keep medicines and button batteries locked away, use stair gates, turn pan handles inwards and keep hot drinks out of reach. Check your home again as they grow.
body_copy.Pstw57: Try bubbles, a library story time, a trip to the park, a cardboard box den or painting with water outside. Free or cheap activities can be the best ones.
body_copy.Pstw58: Regular play dates and groups help your toddler get used to being around other children. Expect some grabbing and tears, as sharing is still a long way off.
body_copy.Pstw59: Keep bedtime routines consistent, plenty of daytime activity and fresh air help, and avoid screens in the hour before bed.
body_copy.Pstw60: Start with turn-taking games between you and your toddler, like rolling a ball back and forth. Use simple language like 'your turn, my turn'.
body_copy.Pstw61: Use their love of copying to help them learn. Let them 'help' with sweeping, wiping or putting things in the washing machine.
body_copy.Pstw62: If your toddler is climbing out of their cot, it's time to make the move for safety. Otherwise, wait until they're ready and keep it exciting and positive.
body_copy.Pstw63: Stay calm, keep them safe and wait it out. Name the feeling, offer a cuddle when they're ready and avoid giving in to demands.
body_copy.Pstw64: Stay calm and keep your toddler safe, but don't try to wake them. They'll usually settle back to sleep on their own. A regular bedtime and enough sleep can help prevent them.
body_copy.Pstw65: Plan playdates around naps, leave time to wind down afterwards and watch for tired signs like eye rubbing or clumsiness.
body_copy.Pstw66: Everyone has an opinion on parenting. Thank people, take what helps and leave the rest. You don't need to explain your choices.
body_copy.Pstw67: There's no perfect age gap. Think about your health, finances, support and how you feel. Talk to your GP if you have questions about your body being ready.
body_copy.Pstw68: Don't add salt to your toddler's food and limit sugary foods and drinks. Water and milk are the best drinks. Check labels on 'toddler' snacks, as some are high in sugar.
body_copy.Pstw69: In England, working parents may be able to get up to 30 hours of funded childcare a week from 9 months. Some 2-year-olds can get 15 free hours, and all 3 and 4 year olds can. Tax-Free Childcare can help with costs too.
body_copy.Pstw70: Your toddler will be offered vaccines at 18 months, including their second MMRV dose. This appointment is new from 2026, so check your GP has it booked.
body_copy.Pstw71: Set up a few simple toys, stay nearby and gradually step back. Start with a few minutes and build up over time.
body_copy.Pstw72: Local groups, classes, apps and nursery gates are all great places to meet other parents. A simple 'shall we go for a coffee?' can be the start of a great friendship.
body_copy.Pstw73: Comparing yourself to others, chasing perfect routines and worrying about every milestone date can all add pressure. Focus on what works for you.
body_copy.Pstw74: Lay out clothes the night before, keep a stocked bag by the door, batch cook and freeze toddler meals, and give simple choices to avoid battles.
body_copy.Pstw75: Is this normal? Is my toddler eating enough? Why won't they sleep? Most worries are shared by lots of parents, and there's support available for all of them.
body_copy.Pstw76: Prepare as much as you can the night before, share drop-offs and pick-ups and make the most of the time you have together.
body_copy.Pstw77: Take turns with night wakings, nap when you can at weekends and keep evenings calm. Talk to your health visitor if night waking is ongoing.
body_copy.Pstw78: Your toddler may know when they have a wet or dirty nappy, tell you they need to go or stay dry for longer. Leaving a potty around so they get used to it is a gentle first step.
body_copy.Pstm19: Offer small portions, eat together and include one food you know they like. Avoid pressure or bribes, and let them decide how much they eat.
body_copy.Pstm20: Keep the routine short and the same every night: bath, pyjamas, story, bed. Offer simple choices, like which pyjamas or which book.
body_copy.Pstm21: Let your toddler see the potty, read potty books together and talk about using the toilet. Dress them in clothes that are easy to pull down.
body_copy.Pstm22: Use a timer for turns, praise sharing when you see it and model it yourself. Put away special toys before friends visit.
body_copy.Pstm23: Let them choose bedding, keep their routine the same and use a bed guard. If they keep getting up, calmly walk them back to bed.
body_copy.Pstm24: Your health visitor will offer a review between 2 and 2 and a half years. They'll look at your child's speech, movement and behaviour, and you can ask anything.
body_copy.Pstm25: Let your toddler help in the kitchen, offer the same food as the rest of the family and keep trying new foods, sometimes 10 to 15 times.
body_copy.Pstm26: Stay calm, keep them safe and don't give in. Spot triggers like hunger and tiredness, and give lots of attention when they're behaving well.
body_copy.Pstm27: Keep rules simple and consistent, explain them briefly and follow through. Focus on what you want them to do, like 'walk inside' instead of 'don't run'.
body_copy.Pstm28: Let your toddler choose books, use silly voices and ask questions about the pictures. Library visits are free and a great way to find new favourites.
body_copy.Pstm29: Puddle jumping, nature walks, collecting leaves and visiting the park are all free and fun. Dress for the weather and let them explore.
body_copy.Pstm30: There's no right number of children. Think about what feels right for your family, your health and your circumstances.
body_copy.Pstm31: It's early, but it's worth knowing how school applications work in your area. Visiting nurseries and schools can help you get a feel for what's out there.
body_copy.Pstm32: Your child will be offered their preschool booster at around 3 years and 4 months. Your GP surgery should contact you, but you can check if it's due.
body_copy.Pstm33: Keep screens off before bed, stick to the same order every night and give a warning before bedtime starts. A sticker chart can help older toddlers.
body_copy.Pstm34: Pack snacks and favourite toys, plan around nap times and choose family-friendly places. Keep your expectations realistic and enjoy the small moments.
body_copy.Pstm35: Keep explanations short, get down to their level and offer choices where you can. Acknowledge their feelings before explaining.
body_copy.Pstm36: In England, all 3 and 4 year olds can get 15 hours of free early education a week from the term after they turn three. Some families can get 30 hours.
body_copy.Pstm37: Listen to their worries, use a night light and keep a calm bedtime routine. Avoid scary stories or screens before bed.
body_copy.Pstm38: Try putting toys away, matching socks, watering plants or setting the table. Praise their effort rather than how perfectly it's done.
body_copy.Pstm39: Keep offering a variety of foods, involve your child in choosing and preparing meals and avoid pressure. Praise trying, not finishing.
body_copy.Pstm40: Offer a wide range of toys and activities and let your child choose what interests them. Avoid labels like 'boys' toys' or 'girls' toys'.
body_copy.Pstm41: Visit schools, read Ofsted reports and talk to other parents. In England, primary applications usually close on 15 January for a September start.
body_copy.Pstm42: Stay calm, avoid punishment and keep offering reminders. Speak to your health visitor or GP if you're worried, especially about constipation.
body_copy.Pstm43: Play turn-taking games, praise sharing and help them use words to ask for things. Board games are great for practising.
body_copy.Pstm44: Be clear and consistent, explain briefly and stick to your answer. Offer alternatives where you can, like 'not today, but we can go to the park'.
body_copy.Pstm45: Plan ahead, use routines and give your child small jobs. Keep a family calendar for nursery, appointments and activities.
body_copy.Pstm46: Plan the week ahead, share responsibilities and make the most of time together. Small rituals, like a bedtime chat, matter more than you think.
body_copy.Pstm47: Give each child one-to-one time, avoid comparisons and help them solve problems together. Step in if anyone gets hurt.
body_copy.Pstm48: Practise skills like putting on shoes, going to the toilet independently and following simple instructions. Talk positively about school.
body_copy.Pstm49: Try painting, playdough, junk modelling with boxes and tubes, or making up stories together.
body_copy.Pstm50: Visit the library, explore parks, build dens with blankets and have picnics in the garden. Free events are often listed on your council website.
body_copy.Pstm51: Give your child time for free play every day. Role play, building, outdoor play and games all help them learn.
body_copy.Pstm52: Keep routines similar between homes, communicate clearly and avoid arguing in front of your child. A shared calendar can help.
body_copy.Pstm53: Try blending frozen banana with a little milk for an easy ice cream. Let your child choose toppings like berries.
body_copy.Pstm54: Get down to their level, make eye contact and repeat back what they've said. Show interest in their stories, however long.
body_copy.Pstm55: Plan meals, buy second-hand clothes and toys and look for free activities. Check you're getting any benefits or support you're entitled to.
body_copy.Pstm56: Listen calmly, help your child name their feelings and talk to their nursery or school if you're worried. Teach them simple ways to respond.
body_copy.Pstm57: Plan ahead, pack snacks and activities and keep some familiar routines. Choose family-friendly places with things to do for all ages.
body_copy.Pstm58: Go on nature walks, build dens, climb at the park or go on a bug hunt. Let them lead the way.
body_copy.Pstm59: Try board games, movie nights, baking or a walk together. Simple activities are often the most memorable.
body_copy.Pstm60: Look back at photos, talk about what they've learned and celebrate how far they've come. Ask what they're looking forward to next.

tip_2.Pstw52: Swap one bottle at a time

title.Pstw10: Still finding your feet? That's normal.
title.Pstw12: The newborn stage is behind you
title.Pstw48: Happy first birthday to you too
title.Pstm32: Staying on top of it all

body_copy.Pstw01: Bleeding after birth, sore stitches and feeling tearful around day three to five are all common. Rest as much as you can and let others take care of the house. Tell your midwife if anything worries you.
body_copy.Pstw02: Feeling weepy and overwhelmed in the first couple of weeks is really common and usually passes. If low feelings last more than two weeks or get worse, talk to your health visitor or GP.
body_copy.Pstw03: Your womb is shrinking back and bleeding should be getting lighter. If bleeding gets heavier, smells unusual or you have a fever, contact your midwife or GP straight away.
body_copy.Pstw04: Even ten minutes for a shower, a cup of tea or a walk around the block can make a difference. Ask your partner, family or friends to take over for a short while each day.
body_copy.Pstw05: Broken nights are hard. Try going to bed earlier, sharing night feeds if you can, and resting rather than doing chores when your baby naps.
body_copy.Pstw06: Your check is a chance to talk about your physical recovery, contraception and how you're feeling emotionally. Be honest, this appointment is for you.
body_copy.Pstw07: Your pelvic floor muscles have worked hard. Gentle squeezes, a few times a day, can help with leaks and recovery. They're easy to do while feeding.
body_copy.Pstw08: You don't need a strict routine yet, but a simple pattern like a bath, feed and bed can help you both. Do whatever works for your family.
body_copy.Pstw09: It can feel like your whole world is your baby right now. Make small time for something that's just yours, like a podcast, a walk or a chat with a friend.
body_copy.Pstw10: Ten weeks in, lots of mums are still running on very little sleep. If something doesn't feel right, physically or emotionally, your GP or health visitor is there to help, and so are our midwives.
body_copy.Pstw11: If your postnatal check went well, you can start building up gentle exercise like walking, swimming once bleeding has stopped, or postnatal classes. Go at your own pace.
body_copy.Pstw12: You've made it through the first three months, which is a huge achievement. Take a moment to notice how far you've both come.
body_copy.Pstw13: If you're struggling to function, tell someone. A partner, friend or relative taking one feed or an early morning can give you a stretch of proper sleep.
body_copy.Pstw14: If you're returning to work later in the year, it's never too early to think about childcare and your options. Keeping in touch days can help ease you back in.
body_copy.Pstw15: Postnatal depression can start any time in the first year. If you feel low, anxious or not like yourself most days, speak to your GP or health visitor.
body_copy.Pstw16: Baby groups, classes or online communities can be a lifeline. Other parents at the same stage understand exactly what you're going through.
body_copy.Pstw17: A new baby changes everything, including your relationship. Make a little time to talk about something other than nappies, even if it's just over a cup of tea.
body_copy.Pstw18: You don't need lots of kit. A highchair, a few soft spoons, a free-flow or open cup and a bib or two are plenty to start.
body_copy.Pstw19: Lifting, feeding and carrying can all take a toll on your back. Try to bring your baby close before lifting and keep your back straight when feeding.
body_copy.Pstw20: If you've been putting your own needs last, try to schedule one small thing a week that's just for you.
body_copy.Pstw21: It's easy to compare your baby, or yourself, to others online. Remember you're only seeing a small part of their day.
body_copy.Pstw22: Lots of mums notice things feel a bit easier around now. If they don't for you, that's okay too, every journey is different.
body_copy.Pstw23: If you're feeling exhausted all the time, mention it to your GP. Low iron and thyroid problems can both be more common after having a baby.
body_copy.Pstw24: Half a year of looking after a tiny person is no small thing. Mark it in a way that feels right, even if it's just a takeaway and an early night.
body_copy.Pstw25: Worrying is part of being a parent. If anxiety is stopping you from sleeping or enjoying things, talk to your GP or health visitor.
body_copy.Pstw26: It's easy to forget to eat yourself. Sitting down together, even with a quick snack, shows your baby how meals work.
body_copy.Pstw27: Sharing a laugh with your baby releases feel-good hormones for both of you. On the tough days, a silly game can reset everyone's mood.
body_copy.Pstw28: Weaning can feel stressful. Remember that up to one year, milk is still their main source of nutrition, so food is about learning and exploring.
body_copy.Pstw29: You don't have to do it all. Make a list of jobs others can do, so when someone asks how they can help, you've got an answer ready.
body_copy.Pstw30: Your baby watches everything you do, which can feel like a lot of pressure. Remember they need a good enough parent, not a perfect one.
body_copy.Pstw31: Remembering appointments, meals, nappies and naps is a lot. Share the planning, not just the jobs, with your partner or support network.
body_copy.Pstw32: Sleep regressions hit parents hard. Take turns with nights if you can, and keep caffeine to the morning so you can sleep when you get the chance.
body_copy.Pstw33: Having a baby who wants only you is lovely and exhausting. Let others build their own bond too, even if there are tears at first.
body_copy.Pstw34: Parenting confidence grows with time. You know your baby better than anyone, so trust what you're seeing and feeling.
body_copy.Pstw35: Take a moment to check in with yourself. If you've been feeling flat or anxious for a while, it's worth talking to your GP or health visitor.
body_copy.Pstw36: Protect your own sleep where you can. A screen-free half hour before bed and going to bed earlier can help you make the most of the time you get.
body_copy.Pstw37: Getting down on the floor with your baby counts as movement for you too. Building a little activity into your day can help your mood and energy.
body_copy.Pstw38: Falls are part of learning, but they can still make your heart race. Know when to get help: if your baby is drowsy, vomits or seems unwell after a bump, seek medical advice.
body_copy.Pstw39: If you're going back to work soon, think about settling-in sessions with your childcare so you both have time to adjust.
body_copy.Pstw40: Talk with your partner or co-parent about how you want to handle boundaries, so your baby gets the same message from both of you.
body_copy.Pstw41: It's lovely to celebrate what your baby is learning. Take a moment to notice what you've learned too.
body_copy.Pstw42: If visits feel stressful, keep them short and on your terms. It's fine to say no to plans that don't work for you right now.
body_copy.Pstw43: Parenting a baby can feel repetitive. A book, podcast or new hobby can give your mind something different to focus on.
body_copy.Pstw44: You know your baby best. If something doesn't feel right, it's always okay to ask for advice, even if you think you're worrying over nothing.
body_copy.Pstw45: Once your baby is on the move, life gets busier. Make sure your home is safe so you can relax a little more.
body_copy.Pstw46: Waiting for answers can be hard. Lean on the people around you, and look for support groups if your child needs extra help.
body_copy.Pstw47: Making new friends as a parent can feel daunting. Saying yes to a coffee after a baby group is a great place to start.
body_copy.Pstw48: This is your first birthday as a parent. Celebrate what you've done this year, the sleepless nights, the firsts and everything in between.
body_copy.Pstw49: Narrating your day out loud might feel strange, but it's one of the best things you can do. Pick a time, like bath or nappy changes, to start.
body_copy.Pstw50: One nap can give you a longer, more predictable break. Use it for rest as well as jobs.
body_copy.Pstw51: Mixed feelings are completely normal. Ask your employer about flexible working if it would help, you have the right to request it from your first day.
body_copy.Pstw52: You've made it through a whole year. Whatever it looked like for you, you should feel proud.
body_copy.Pstw53: Ticking off milestones can be fun, but don't let it cause stress. Your toddler is doing things in their own time.
body_copy.Pstw54: Toddlers are on the go all day. Make sure you're eating well and staying hydrated to keep your energy up.
body_copy.Pstw55: Joining in with play can be fun for you too. Let yourself be silly, it's good for your mood.
body_copy.Pstw56: Constant supervision is tiring. A safe space where your toddler can play freely gives you a break from saying no.
body_copy.Pstw57: Raising a little one is expensive. Check you're getting any support you're entitled to, like Child Benefit.
body_copy.Pstw58: Friendships can change after a baby. It's okay to lean into new ones while keeping the old ones going in smaller ways.
body_copy.Pstw59: If sleep has been tough for a long time, it can affect your mood. Talk to your GP if you're struggling.
body_copy.Pstw60: Toddler behaviour can test anyone's patience. Take a breath, and remember they're not being naughty, they're learning.
body_copy.Pstw61: Cold cups of tea, never weeing alone and a bag full of snacks. The small things are part of it, and you're far from alone.
body_copy.Pstw62: Big changes like moving beds can mean some disrupted nights. Try to avoid making the move at the same time as other big changes.
body_copy.Pstw63: It's normal to feel frustrated too. If you need to, make sure your toddler is safe and step away for a minute to breathe.
body_copy.Pstw64: Night terrors are scary to watch. Remind yourself that your toddler isn't aware of them, even though you are.
body_copy.Pstw65: Playdates are as much for you as your toddler. Choose ones that feel easy and enjoyable.
body_copy.Pstw66: Judgement can sting, especially when you're tired. Surround yourself with people who build you up.
body_copy.Pstw67: Whether you want another baby now, later or not at all, it's your choice. Don't feel pressured by others' timelines.
body_copy.Pstw68: Don't stress about perfect meals every day. Look at what your toddler eats across a week rather than a single day.
body_copy.Pstw69: Childcare can be one of the biggest family costs. Check what support you can get before making decisions.
body_copy.Pstw70: Look at how much your toddler has learned. Take a moment to recognise your role in that.
body_copy.Pstw71: Juggling work and a toddler at home is tough. Be realistic about what you can get done, and plan focused work for naps or childcare days.
body_copy.Pstw72: Friends who understand what you're going through can make a huge difference to how you feel.
body_copy.Pstw73: There's no one right way to parent. If your family is happy and safe, you're doing a great job.
body_copy.Pstw74: Shortcuts aren't cheating, they're smart. Save your energy for the moments that matter.
body_copy.Pstw75: If something's on your mind, ask. There's no such thing as a silly question when it comes to your child.
body_copy.Pstw76: Balancing work and parenting is challenging. Be kind to yourself and let go of what doesn't matter.
body_copy.Pstw77: Long-term lack of sleep is hard. Prioritise rest where you can and don't feel guilty about it.
body_copy.Pstw78: There's no prize for potty training early. Waiting until they're ready usually means it's quicker and less stressful.
body_copy.Pstm19: Mealtime battles are draining. Remember it's your job to offer the food, and their job to decide how much to eat.
body_copy.Pstm20: Bedtime battles eat into your time. Once your toddler is settled, try to switch off and do something for you.
body_copy.Pstm21: Choose a time when there are no big changes ahead for potty training, like a new sibling or moving house.
body_copy.Pstm22: Toddler squabbles at the park can feel embarrassing, but every parent there has been through it.
body_copy.Pstm23: The first few weeks in a big bed can be bumpy. Stay consistent, and it will settle.
body_copy.Pstm24: Two years of parenting is a real achievement. Take time to think about how much you've grown too.
body_copy.Pstm25: Family meals don't have to be fancy. Eating together, even a few times a week, is what matters.
body_copy.Pstm26: Tantrums are tough on parents too. It's okay to feel frustrated, step back and take a breath.
body_copy.Pstm27: Boundaries work best when everyone caring for your child is consistent. Agree the main rules together.
body_copy.Pstm28: Story time can be a calm, cosy part of your day too. Enjoy the chance to slow down together.
body_copy.Pstm29: Getting outdoors can help your mood and energy as much as theirs.
body_copy.Pstm30: Family size is a personal decision. Don't let anyone else's opinion rush you.
body_copy.Pstm31: Planning for school can feel like a big step. Take it one bit at a time.
body_copy.Pstm32: Keeping track of appointments can be tricky. A shared calendar can help.
body_copy.Pstm33: Once your toddler is asleep, try to give yourself some proper downtime.
body_copy.Pstm34: Holidays with little ones aren't always restful, but they can still be fun. Share the load so everyone gets a break.
body_copy.Pstm35: It can feel like you're repeating yourself all day, but it's working, even when it doesn't seem like it.
body_copy.Pstm36: Three years of parenting is something to be proud of. Treat yourself as well as your little one.
body_copy.Pstm37: Your calm presence helps your child feel safe. Reassure them that you're nearby.
body_copy.Pstm38: Their help might slow you down now, but it builds good habits for the future.
body_copy.Pstm39: Mealtimes don't need to be perfect. Look at what your child eats over a week.
body_copy.Pstm40: Encouraging your child to be themselves builds confidence and self-esteem.
body_copy.Pstm41: Choosing a school can feel overwhelming. Trust your instincts about where your child will be happy.
body_copy.Pstm42: Setbacks don't mean you've done something wrong. Most children get there in their own time.
body_copy.Pstm43: Sharing is a skill that takes years to learn. Every bit of practice helps.
body_copy.Pstm44: Saying no can be hard, especially when you're tired. Remember it's okay to stick to your decision.
body_copy.Pstm45: It's easy to put yourself last. Try to keep one thing each week that's just for you.
body_copy.Pstm46: Balancing work and family is tough. Be kind to yourself and focus on what matters most.
body_copy.Pstm47: Squabbles are exhausting. Remember it's normal and they're learning important skills.
body_copy.Pstm48: Four years of parenting is amazing. Take time to celebrate what you've achieved.
body_copy.Pstm49: Creative play can be messy, but it's worth it. Cover the table and let them explore.
body_copy.Pstm50: Family costs add up. Look for free activities and check you're getting any support you're entitled to.
body_copy.Pstm51: Joining in with play is a great way to connect with your child.
body_copy.Pstm52: Co-parenting can be challenging. Look for support if you need it, from friends, family or professionals.
body_copy.Pstm53: Cooking together doesn't have to be perfect. Enjoy the time together.
body_copy.Pstm54: Small moments of connection make a big difference. Even five minutes of focused time each day helps.
body_copy.Pstm55: Money worries can be stressful. Free advice is available from organisations like Citizens Advice.
body_copy.Pstm56: It's upsetting when your child is hurt. Talking to staff early can help solve problems quickly.
body_copy.Pstm57: Holidays with children aren't always restful, but they can be fun. Share responsibilities so everyone gets a break.
body_copy.Pstm58: Time outside can boost your mood too.
body_copy.Pstm59: It's the small, everyday moments that children remember.
body_copy.Pstm60: Five years of parenting is an incredible achievement. Thank you for letting us be part of the journey.
